spikes.fact: Does a `permissions.allow` rule such as `Bash(node <path>/merge-pr.js:*)` in `~/.claude/settings.json` stop the permission refusal of Workflow relay subagents when the session runs in auto mode? Subagents: each subagent action goes through the same decision order and the same allow and block rules as the parent session, and a subagent's permissionMode frontmatter is ignored. The docs do not mention Workflow, dynamic workflow, or background runs, so they do not confirm whether Workflow relay subagents are covered. The ":*" suffix in the rule is not the form shown in the current docs, which put a space before the wildcard (for example Bash(npm test *)). The docs do not say whether the ":*" form matches, so that is unverified. Protected-path writes are not pre-approved by permissions.allow rules in settings files. The autoMode key is documented only in outline (autoMode.allow, autoMode.environment, claude auto-mode defaults); the full schema is on a page I did not read. (b) Not settled. The docs contain nothing about --dry-run of a Workflow or a merge script, or why a dry-run would pass where the real run is refused. spikes.fact: How does Claude Code match Bash permission rules? Does `:*` or ` *` require a word boundary? Are `~` or symlinks expanded or resolved in a rule's path? Does the bare rule `Bash` or `Bash(*)` allow every command?
spikes.answer:
(a) Word boundary: Yes for a trailing wildcard written with a space before it, and for the `:*` form (which the docs say is equivalent). `Bash(ls *)` matches `ls -la` and bare `ls`, but not `lsof`. `Bash(ls*)` with no space matches both `ls -la` and `lsof`. A `*` anywhere else (start, middle) matches any text including spaces, with no boundary. A rule with no `*` matches one exact command. `:*` is only recognized at the end of a pattern; `Bash(git:* push)` treats the colon as a literal. Also, `Bash(* --help *)` matches `npm --help x` but not bare `npm --help`, since the bare-command match only applies when the trailing `*` is the rule's only wildcard. Matching is on the command text Claude writes, after compound commands are split and wrappers stripped. Commands in a different form (e.g. `/usr/bin/curl`, `sh -c '...'`, `git -C . push`) are not matched.
(b) `~` and symlinks: The docs describe `~/path` only for Read and Edit path rules (gitignore-style: `~/path` = path from home directory, e.g. `Read(~/Documents/*.pdf)` matches `/Users/alice/Documents/*.pdf`). The docs' symlink section says that for a file path Claude requests through a symbolic link, the permission check covers both the requested path and the file it resolves to (macOS, Linux, Windows; Windows junctions too). That section is about file-path permission checks; the docs do not state whether Bash rule text is tilde-expanded or symlink-resolved. Bash rule matching is described as literal text matching, so no expansion is documented for it. Note the docs do give `$HOME/bin/*` as an example of a wildcarded path that auto mode drops, but no expansion rule is stated.
(c) Bare `Bash` and `Bash(*)`: Both match all Bash commands. The docs say `Bash(*)` is equivalent to `Bash`. As an allow rule, that means every Bash command runs without a prompt (subject to deny and ask rules, which take precedence, and to auto-mode handling: in auto mode, blanket `Bash(*)` allow rules are dropped on entering auto mode). As a deny rule, either form removes the tool from Claude's context entirely. Separately, a sandboxing note says a bare `Bash` ask rule or `Bash(*)` ask is skipped for commands that run sandboxed, but still applies outside the sandbox, and not in plan mode.
Evaluation order: deny, then ask, then allow; first match wins; specificity does not change order.

spikes.fact: Do a `permissions.ask` rule, managed settings (`/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json`) or `--settings` flags change whether a non-interactive relay subagent is allowed to run a command that the three settings files the spec reads would allow?
spikes.answer: Partly settled, not fully. Per the docs: (1) Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow; the first match decides. A matching ask rule prompts even when a more specific allow rule also matches, so a permissions.ask rule overrides an allow rule from the three settings files for the same command. A matching deny rule blocks regardless of allow. (2) Precedence: managed settings are highest, then --settings (command line), then project local, shared project, and user. Nothing in user, project, local or --settings overrides a managed key. Lists such as permissions.allow merge across non-managed scopes, and managed allow rules still apply alongside user/project allow rules unless allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly is set. So a managed file or --settings flag can add or remove rules, but a managed deny or ask cannot be overridden by an allow in the other files. (3) Non-interactive: the docs say that in dontAsk mode, calls that would prompt are auto-denied, and that for a -p run with nothing to answer a prompt, Claude Code denies the call (stated for org-set ask on claude.ai connector tools). Setting permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting true (honored from ~/.claude/settings.json or --settings even when managed says false) makes calls that would wait on a prompt be denied, so an unattended session keeps working. The docs do not explicitly state how a subagent (Agent tool) handles ask prompts; no source I read settles that case directly. Also, the managed-settings.json file does not exist on this machine (checked 2026-11-25), so only the documented precedence applies to it.

spikes.fact: Does the Workflow runtime enforce the `required` keys of the JSON schema passed to `agent()`, so a critic cannot return a verdict without `items`?
spikes.answer: Yes, per the Claude Code Workflows docs: the output is checked against the schema and retried; after five failed attempts the call errors instead of returning a verdict missing a required key. Caveat: the docs do not state the per-key rule verbatim; it is shown by a user bug report (#70645). Bug #76901 shows a schema-satisfying placeholder can be returned after retry exhaustion, so required keys are enforced by type, not content (e.g. items could be a near-empty value unless minLength or pattern is set).
